 The next big travel nightmare could start at the TSA check-in line
 By Chris Isidore 
 PUBLISHED Nov 21, 2026, 6:00 AM ET 
 A passenger passes a plane waiting at the terminal of Reagan Washington National Airport, Washington, DC, on November 13, 2026, after a rare ground stop of all flights across the country. The next travel hassle for passengers could come if a federal government shutdown creates a shortage of security screeners and air traffic controllers just before the year-end holiday travel period. 
 Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images

 The next travel nightmare could have nothing to do with technology outages and everything to do with political gridlock.
 Funding for the federal government, including the Transportation Security Administration and the Federal Aviation Administration, is set to expire on December 12. That means just two weeks before the holiday travel rush, security screeners and air traffic controllers could be expected to show up for work without pay.
 In the past, that’s resulted in staffing shortages and headaches for travelers — hours-long lines at TSA screening and canceled flights due to a lack of controllers.
 An airport employee holds a sign indicating the end of the line in March 2026 at the Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport. The shutdown caused long lines at TSA security points due a shortage of workers to screen passengers. 
 Daniel Heuer/Reuters 
 Sudden bad weather can turn even a fully staffed holiday travel period into a nightmare, which was the case with the Southwest meltdown a few years ago. If that happens, experts say passengers could be facing the worst travel period on record.
 “December holidays are a melting pot for everything that could go wrong. You have snow, you have airlines over-scheduling to the max. There’s no room for anything to go wrong,” Zach Griff, author of airline newsletter From the Tray Table, told CNN. “Could you imagine if TSA and FAA are not staffed? It would be a disaster.”
 Real threat of a shutdown
 No one in the federal government wants to cause a holiday travel disaster.
 Both political parties are eager to avoid a debilitating government shutdown, especially at a time when there’s intense nationwide anxiety about technology outages. The Trump administration also hopes to avert a shutdown, sources familiar with plans told CNN . The preferred scenario among party leaders is to pass another stopgap funding bill.
 However, the funding fight is effectively frozen until the Senate Democrats’ internal leadership election on December 1, multiple lawmakers and senior aides in both parties told CNN, and then it will likely take weeks to reach an agreement.
 The Washington Monument seen in the distance as passengers and planes wait at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, in Arlington, Virginia, just outside Washington, DC. Passengers could face long TSA screening lines and canceled flights if a government shutdown two weeks before Christmas causes a shortage of TSA workers and air traffic controllers. 
 Aaron Schwartz/AFP/Getty Images 
 That’s why leaders of the unions representing TSA screeners and air traffic controllers are very worried that their members will soon be told they will not be paid during the holiday season.
 “We take the flying public very seriously. We want them to get to their loved ones during the holidays,” said Hydrick Thomas, one of the council presidents for the TSA’s union, the American Federation of Government Employees, told CNN. The AFGE has been in a battle with the Trump administration since early last year, when it issued an executive order no longer recognizing the union or its contract.
 “When you shut us down and not pay us, that’s saying you don’t even care about the American people,” Thomas added.
 The air traffic control system is already severely understaffed, another stressor for controllers who are stuck using aging equipment, according to Nick Daniels, president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association.
 Systemwide outages like the one last week just call attention to problems that have existed for years, he said.
 “People are the core of the system, and they’re the ones that need to be recognized for the efforts of what they did (during the FAA ground stop),” Daniels said. “But controllers are again facing having to go to work and not getting paid. Let us do our jobs, quit holding our paychecks ransom.”
 Air Traffic Control tower at Chicago O'Hare International Airport. 
 Jim Vondruska/Reuters 
 Neither the TSA nor the FAA responded to questions from CNN about contingency plans should there be another government shutdown.
 During the last shutdown, staffing shortages at air traffic control centers resulted in canceled flights, as the FAA restricted the number at some busier airports, limiting travel options. TSA shortages led to lines that lasted for hours, some expanding outside terminal buildings.
 But union leaders said those who didn’t come to work didn’t have a choice. They didn’t have enough money for childcare or to pay for gas. Some TSA agents, who are paid as little as $40,700 a year, are already stretched thin financially.
 “People did what they needed to do,” said LaShanda Palmer, president of the Philadelphia AFGE. “There are people who are still recuperating from the last two (shutdowns), people who lost their cars. We were used as pawns in the Civil War where we should never have been.”
 Holiday travel surge
 The holiday travel period is typically one of the busiest of the year, and this year will be no different. The major US airlines are all already reporting strong bookings.
 Last year, between the Saturday before Christmas and the Sunday after New Year’s, TSA said agents screened 140,000 more passengers per day than on average.
 Airlines schedule the maximum number of flights during the holidays to meet that demand. But high fuel costs have forced carriers to trim their schedules, cutting less profitable flights. That means if any flights are canceled due to a shortage of air traffic controllers, passengers would likely have trouble finding available seats on other flights.
 People look at the departure board at Miami International Airport after the FAA announced a nationwide ground stop on November 13, 2026. The next travel problem for passengers could come in December if a government shutdown causes a shortage of TSA screeners and air traffic controllers. 
 Joe Raedle/Getty Images 
 Union leaders say that both TSA and air traffic controllers take their jobs very seriously. Many say their job is critical to protecting the public.
 The TSA, created in the wake of the September 11 terrorist attacks, just celebrated its 25th anniversary this past week. AFGE’s Thomas said his members’ dedication is likely one reason there has not been a repeat of those kinds of attacks.
 “I want people to look back and say, ‘How many passengers lost their lives (since 9/11)? How many flights fell out of the sky because we failed the country?’” Thomas said. “We (TSA screeners) didn’t fail the country. I think the politicians are failing us.”
